name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,603

clue.text: Loved returning to embrace new hero in Eliot

indicators.note: something returning goes back the way it came, so the word is read from right to left
to embrace is to wrap arms around, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: loved in the sense of worshipped
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone fond of George Eliot's fiction comes back to welcome a fresh hero from her novels.
explanation.walkthrough: Daniel DERONDA is the title hero of George Eliot's last novel; ADORED turned round is DERODA, which takes N in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel Deronda is the title character and protagonist of a George Eliot novel published in 1876.

clue.text: Removes risk element from brilliant exercises

blocks.note: slang for excellent or cool
to exercise a power is to use it

explanation.surface: Someone takes the danger out of a dazzling workout routine.
explanation.walkthrough: DEF is slang for excellent, borrowed from hip-hop; exercises is a verb here, as in exercising a right.
explanation.definitionFit: To defuse a bomb or tense situation is literally to take away the part that could cause harm.

clue.text: Varied resources here to cover French study update

indicators.note: things varied are changed about, so these letters come in a new order
to cover something is to go over and around it, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
FR is the standard abbreviation for French

explanation.surface: A notice says a range of materials is available to support a programme of French study.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged thirteen letters are REESHERCOURSE, and FR slips in after the first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A refresher course is a short programme of training that brings someone's existing knowledge up to date.

clue.text: Elvish giant oddly dismissive over nothing

indicators.note: being dismissive of the odd positions throws them out, so only the even-numbered letters stay
in a down clue, over suggests turning upside down, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A huge creature from Tolkien-style fantasy waves away the idea of emptiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' normally keeps the odd letters; here 'dismissive' throws them away, leaving the even ones L, I, H, I, N.
explanation.definitionFit: Nihil is the Latin word for nothing, familiar from phrases such as nihil obstat and from nihilism.

clue.text: Strange approach taken about year books

indicators.note: something strange is out of its usual form, so these letters are reordered
taken around something means placed so it surrounds it

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
Y is the standard abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: An odd way of tackling a whole year's reading list.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters come out as APOCR-PHA with Y placed in the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apocrypha are the biblical books of uncertain authority, included in some Bibles but left out of others.

clue.text: Fine intelligence associated with Prince Charlie

blocks.note: Prince Hal, Shakespeare's young Henry V
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
quickness of mind

explanation.surface: Bonnie Prince Charlie is credited with a sharp mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince Charlie' reads as one name, but Prince is HAL and Charlie stands alone as the definition; in British slang a charlie is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a right charlie in British English means they are a fool, the same as calling them a halfwit.

clue.text: Answer found in search for plague

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for answer
a hunt is a search

explanation.surface: Scientists hunting for a cure for a deadly epidemic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plague' looks like the disease being searched for, but it is a verb meaning to trouble persistently.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs describe something that keeps tormenting a person, as memories or worries do.

clue.text: Squire needs way to cross Blue River

indicators.note: a road crossing an area runs across it, here taken as lying around the thing it spans

blocks.note: a lane is a narrow road or way
feeling blue is feeling down
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A country gentleman wants a path across the Blue River on his estate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue River' looks like a place name, but blue means sad, and River is just R.
explanation.definitionFit: A squire was the chief landowner of an English village, so the title and the role are near-synonyms.

clue.text: Watts set out riding magnificent horse in town

indicators.note: letters spread out are scattered and gathered up again in a fresh order

blocks.note: W is the symbol for watts
taken as written, to be rearranged
a rider is on the horse
super means excellent
a mare is a female horse

explanation.surface: A man called Watts sets off on a splendid horse through town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watts' looks like a person's name, but it is the unit of power, abbreviated W. Weston-super-Mare is an English seaside resort in Somerset.
explanation.definitionFit: Weston-super-Mare is a seaside resort town on the Bristol Channel coast in Somerset, England.

clue.text: Elephants endlessly compact eating Welsh flower

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped
whatever eats something takes it inside, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: terse means compact or concise, here losing its last letter
a flower is something that flows, a river; the Usk runs through South Wales

explanation.surface: Elephants squashed together munching a daffodil, the Welsh national flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh flower' suggests the leek or daffodil, but a flower here is a river, the Usk.
explanation.definitionFit: A tusker is an elephant or other animal with prominent tusks, especially a large male.

clue.text: Animated fun with Scottish film showing collaborators

indicators.note: something animated is moving about, so these letters are set in motion into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cartoon comedy from Scotland is being screened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Animated' reads as describing a cartoon, but it is the signal to rearrange all three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Fifth columnists are people inside a country who secretly work for and help an enemy, that is, traitorous collaborators.

clue.text: Archaeologist Croft tucking into fish that's suspect?

indicators.note: tucking into something means slipping inside it

blocks.note: Lara Croft, the archaeologist heroine of the Tomb Raider games
a smelt is a small fish

explanation.surface: The video-game explorer eats a dubious piece of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucking into' suggests eating, but it means going inside. 'Suspect' looks like an adjective about the fish; it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To smell a rat is an idiom for sensing that something is wrong or someone is being deceitful.

clue.text: Wizard seen here complete in bracing sea air

blocks.note: the land where the Wizard of Oz is found
one in the sense of whole or undivided

explanation.surface: A magician spotted doing his act at a breezy seaside resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wizard seen here' is a little cryptic definition of a place: the Wizard of Oz lives in Oz.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh seaside air is popularly called ozone in Britain, from the old belief that the gas made it invigorating.

clue.text: Unstressed syllable in school was cut

indicators.note: a cut word has been trimmed, so it loses its last letter

blocks.note: SCH is a standard abbreviation for school
the word trimmed of its final letter

explanation.surface: A weak syllable got dropped during a school lesson on pronunciation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like a verb about the syllable, but it trims the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The schwa is the neutral vowel sound heard in unstressed syllables, like the first sound of 'about'.

clue.text: Cunning fellows housed in suitable accommodation

indicators.note: whatever is housed in something lives inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: apt means fitting or suitable
art in the sense of craft or guile
fellows are men

explanation.surface: Crafty characters have been put up in a decent place to live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cunning' looks like an adjective for the fellows, but it is a noun here, art as in artfulness.
explanation.definitionFit: An apartment is a flat, a set of rooms where someone lives, so it is a kind of lodging.

clue.text: Professional revealed spiritual knowledge in forecast

blocks.note: short for professional
gnosis is mystical or spiritual knowledge, the root of Gnosticism

explanation.surface: An expert discloses mystic insight while making a prediction.
explanation.walkthrough: GNOSIS is a Greek word for knowledge, used in English for spiritual or esoteric insight.
explanation.definitionFit: A prognosis is a prediction of how something, usually an illness, is likely to develop in future.

clue.text: Boat from Oxford University set off

blocks.note: the initials of Oxford University
to trigger an alarm is to set it off

explanation.surface: The Oxford University crew's boat pushes off from the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' suggests a boat departing, but it means to trigger something.
explanation.definitionFit: An outrigger is a boat, such as a canoe or racing shell, fitted with a projecting float or rowlock frame.

clue.text: Target man flying Spitfire

indicators.note: flying letters are scattered through the air and land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An enemy pilot is the target of a man flying a Spitfire, the British wartime fighter plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spitfire' looks like the aircraft, but with a lower-case sense it means a fiery-tempered person.
explanation.definitionFit: A spitfire is a hot-tempered, quarrelsome person, especially a woman, which is exactly what a termagant is.

clue.text: Member consuming wine asks for snack

indicators.note: to consume is to take inside, so one piece swallows the other

blocks.note: a toe is a member, a limb or part of the body
Asti is an Italian sparkling wine

explanation.surface: A club member drinking wine orders something light to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a club member, but it is a body part. A toastie is British for a toasted sandwich.
explanation.definitionFit: A toastie is a toasted sandwich, a light quick meal eaten between proper meals.

clue.text: Become ready to eat carp — no good before noon

indicators.note: having no good means losing the letter that stands for good

blocks.note: to carp is to gripe or complain, and gripe loses G for good
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: A carp caught for lunch is no good to eat until midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carp' looks like the fish, but it is the verb meaning to complain, which gives GRIPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit that ripens matures until it is soft, sweet and fit to be eaten.

clue.text: Setter flips about changed clue for atomic base

indicators.note: something that flips turns over, so the letters run the opposite way
changed letters are altered in order
about means around, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: the sun is something that sets each evening
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler reverses a rewritten clue about atoms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' would usually mean the compiler, giving ME or I; here it is the sun, which sets.
explanation.definitionFit: The nucleus is the dense central core of an atom, around which the electrons are arranged.

clue.text: U-boat on the move nearby

indicators.note: letters on the move shift position, ending in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A wartime submarine is moving somewhere close at hand.
explanation.walkthrough: A U-boat is a German submarine; its five letters rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is about is around or in the vicinity, as in 'is the manager about?'

clue.text: Cheap items almost free in black taxi drivers' association

indicators.note: almost all of a word means it stops one letter short
one piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black
to rid is to free, here missing its last letter
a cab is a taxi
the Royal Automobile Club, a British motoring organisation

explanation.surface: A cabbies' union of London black taxi drivers offers bargain goods nearly for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black taxi' reads as a London cab, but black is just B and taxi is CAB; the shortened word fits between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Bric-a-brac means miscellaneous small ornaments and trinkets of little value, often sold cheaply at fairs.

clue.text: Milk from humble educator

indicators.note: taking letters from a phrase means drawing them out of the run of text

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A modest schoolteacher provides milk for the class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Milk' looks like a drink, but it is a verb, to exploit or drain someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To bleed someone dry and to milk them are both idioms for extracting money or resources relentlessly.

clue.text: Poet in uniform in old British colony

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: Aden, in present-day Yemen, was a British colony until 1967
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A soldier-poet in uniform serves in a former outpost of the Empire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' suggests military dress, but it is the radio code word for the letter U.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden was a major Anglo-American poet of the twentieth century, author of 'Funeral Blues'.

clue.text: Contest in which all runners finish tied?

definitions.text: Contest in which all runners finish tied?

blocks.clueFragment: Contest in which all runners finish tied?
blocks.note: surface reading: a race where every competitor crosses the line at once, a dead heat
setter's reading: the runners end up with their legs bound to a partner's

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tied' means level in the race sense; the setter means physically tied together, ankle to ankle in pairs.
explanation.definitionFit: In this sports-day event pairs of runners have adjacent legs bound together and run as one unit.

clue.text: Chosen people news boss put in office

blocks.note: the elect are those chosen, especially by God for salvation
ED is short for editor, the head of a newspaper

explanation.surface: Those selected appoint a newspaper chief to a post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chosen' wants to be the definition, but 'Chosen people' is one unit and the definition is at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has been voted into a post or position of authority has been elected.

clue.text: Team runs to Plantagenet stronghold

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
Angers in Anjou was the seat of the Angevin counts, ancestors of the Plantagenet kings

explanation.surface: A sports side races to a medieval royal castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Angers is a French city whose counts of Anjou founded the Plantagenet line of English kings.
explanation.definitionFit: Rangers is a Glasgow football club, and several other sports sides share the name.
